In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rapid method for the detection of enterotoxins in clinical specimens.
the development of ELISAs for the detection of antigens that are associated with adhesion of enterotoxicienic E. coli to the small intestine of humans and other animals.
the development of ELISAs to detect antigens of E. coli adhesins and the application of these assays to the study of E. coli isolated in Bangladesh.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antigens of CFA/I, CFA/III (CS1, 2), and PCF8775 (CS4, 5) were detected in more than 50% of strains of enterotoxician E. coli from both Bangladesh and Thailand.
the antigens were detected more frequently by ELISA than in immunodiffusions and that the adhesion factors were associated with strains producing enterotoxins, particularly heat-stable toxin.
the antigens CFA/I, CFA/ II (CS1, 2 and 3), PCF8775 (CS4, 5 and 6) are associated mainly with enterotoxigenicity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ELISA is a more sensitive technique for detecting adhesion antigens than immunodiffusion and that these antigens are associated mainly with strains that carry heat-stable enterotoxin genes.
the antigens CFA/I, CFA/ II, and PCF8775 can be detected in more specimens of E. colifrom the environment and from patients with diarrhea than by other serological methods.
the ELISA is a useful technique for the rapid detection of adhesion factors in E. coli.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ELISA is a more sensitive technique for detection of adhesion factors than immunodiffusion and that the antigens are present in a significant number of strains that are enterotoxigenically active.
adhesion factors of E. coli are not always associated with the ability to produce toxins.
adhesion antigens can be detected by ELISA more easily and more quickly than by other methods.
